subproblem.title: Orthonormal basis adapted to a linear functional: α(u_0) = ‖α‖ and α(u_j) = 0 for j ≠ 0 (parent Steps 4–5)
subproblem.statement: For every P ∈ ℕ and every continuous linear functional α : ℝ^P → ℝ (Eucl P →L[ℝ] ℝ) there is an orthonormal basis u = (u_0,…,u_{P−1}) of ℝ^P, indexed by Fin P, such that for every j ∈ Fin P: α(u_j) = ‖α‖ (the operator norm) if j = 0, and α(u_j) = 0 if j ≠ 0. No hypothesis α ≠ 0 is needed: for α = 0 the standard basis works.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (α : Eucl P →L[ℝ] ℝ), ∃ u : OrthonormalBasis (Fin P) ℝ (Eucl P), ∀ j : Fin P, α (u j) = if (j : ℕ) = 0 then ‖α‖ else 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, Steps 4–5 (the trivial case α = 0 and the adapted orthonormal basis).

Claim. For every P and every continuous linear functional α : ℝ^P → ℝ, there is an orthonormal basis u = (u_0,…,u_{P−1}) of ℝ^P indexed by [P] := {0,…,P−1} such that, for every j ∈ [P], α(u_j) = ‖α‖ if j = 0 and α(u_j) = 0 if j ≠ 0. Here ‖α‖ is the operator norm.

1. (Case α = 0.) Then ‖α‖ = 0. Take u := e, the standard basis, which is orthonormal. For every j, α(e_j) = 0; this equals ‖α‖ = 0 if j = 0 and equals 0 if j ≠ 0. This case includes P = 0, where [P] is empty and the condition is vacuous.

2. (Case α ≠ 0: Riesz vector.) By the Riesz representation on ℝ^P there is a ∈ ℝ^P with α(z) = ⟨a, z⟩ for all z; namely a := (InnerProductSpace.toDual ℝ ℝ^P)⁻¹ α. Moreover |a| = ‖α‖. By Cauchy–Schwarz, |α(z)| ≤ |a||z| for all z, so ‖α‖ ≤ |a|. Also |a|² = α(a) ≤ ‖α‖|a|, so |a| ≤ ‖α‖ (trivial if a = 0). Equivalently, the Riesz map is a linear isometry. Since α ≠ 0, a ≠ 0, so |a| > 0.

3. (P ≥ 1.) ℝ^0 = {0}, so the existence of a ≠ 0 forces P ≥ 1. Hence 0 ∈ [P].

4. (Extension to an orthonormal basis.) v := a/|a| satisfies |v| = 1, so the one-member family (v), indexed by {0} ⊆ [P], is orthonormal. Since dim ℝ^P = P = #[P], this family extends to an orthonormal basis u of ℝ^P indexed by [P] with u_0 = v. This is Gram–Schmidt; in Mathlib, apply Orthonormal.exists_orthonormalBasis_extension_of_card_eq to s := {0} and the constant family j ↦ v, using finrank ℝ ℝ^P = P = Fintype.card (Fin P).

5. (Values.) α(u_0) = ⟨a, a/|a|⟩ = |a|²/|a| = |a| = ‖α‖. For j ≠ 0 we have a = |a|·u_0, hence α(u_j) = ⟨a, u_j⟩ = |a|·⟨u_0, u_j⟩ = 0, because u is orthonormal and u_0 ⊥ u_j for j ≠ 0.

6. (Conclusion.) In both cases α(u_j) = (‖α‖ if j = 0, else 0) for all j ∈ [P]. ∎

Formalization pointers: InnerProductSpace.toDual_symm_apply (⟨(toDual ℝ E).symm α, x⟩ = α x), and the isometry property of toDual for |a| = ‖α‖. Orthonormal.exists_orthonormalBasis_extension_of_card_eq takes hv : Orthonormal ℝ (s.domRestrict v). Use OrthonormalBasis.orthonormal for ⟨u_0, u_j⟩ = 0. In case 1, EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin P) ℝ works.
proof_key_steps: α = 0: ‖α‖ = 0, and the standard basis satisfies the condition.
α ≠ 0: there is a Riesz vector a with α = ⟨a,·⟩ and |a| = ‖α‖ > 0; in particular P ≥ 1.
Extend the unit vector a/|a|, placed at index 0, to an orthonormal basis u of ℝ^P (dim ℝ^P = P).

audit.reason: The zero-functional case includes P = 0. Otherwise the Riesz vector forces P > 0; extending its normalization at index zero and applying orthogonality gives all required values. The natural-number index test in Lean correctly expresses the prose without requiring an inhabitant of Fin 0. No hypothesis is missing.

subproblem.title: Adapted-family estimate: Σ^<_u((α∧γ)²) ≤ c²·Σ^<_u(γ²) when α(u_0) = c and α(u_j) = 0 for j ≠ 0 (parent Steps 6–7)
subproblem.statement: For all P, m ∈ ℕ, every continuous linear functional α : ℝ^P → ℝ, every m-covector γ on ℝ^P, every family u = (u_0,…,u_{P−1}) of vectors of ℝ^P (not necessarily orthonormal) and every c ∈ ℝ such that α(u_j) = c for j = 0 and α(u_j) = 0 for j ≠ 0 (j ∈ Fin P), the following holds. Let α∧γ := alternatizeUncurryFin(α.smulRight γ), so that (α∧γ)(w_0,…,w_m) = Σ_i (−1)^i α(w_i)·γ(w_0,…,ŵ_i,…,w_m). Then Σ_{I : {0,…,m} → [P] strictly increasing} ((α∧γ)(u_{I(0)},…,u_{I(m)}))² ≤ c²·Σ_{J : {0,…,m−1} → [P] strictly increasing} γ(u_{J(0)},…,u_{J(m−1)})². In Lean both sums run over all maps, with summand 0 for maps that are not strictly increasing.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (α : Eucl P →L[ℝ] ℝ) (γ : Covector (Eucl P) m) (u : Fin P → Eucl P) (c : ℝ), (∀ j : Fin P, α (u j) = if (j : ℕ) = 0 then c else 0) → (∑ I : Fin (m + 1) → Fin P, if StrictMono I then (ContinuousAlternatingMap.alternatizeUncurryFin (α.smulRight γ) (fun i => u (I i))) ^ 2 else 0) ≤ c ^ 2 * ∑ I : Fin m → Fin P, if StrictMono I then (γ (fun i => u (I i))) ^ 2 else 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, Steps 6–7. Here ‖α‖ is replaced by an arbitrary constant c, and the adapted orthonormal basis by an arbitrary family u satisfying the value hypothesis; orthonormality is not used in this part.

Notation. [P] := {0,…,P−1}. u = (u_0,…,u_{P−1}) is a family of vectors of ℝ^P, α : ℝ^P → ℝ is continuous linear, γ is an m-covector and c ∈ ℝ. Hypothesis (H): α(u_j) = c if j = 0 and α(u_j) = 0 if j ≠ 0. Put α∧γ := alternatizeUncurryFin(α.smulRight γ), an (m+1)-covector. For I : {0,…,m} → [P] put u_I := (u_{I(0)},…,u_{I(m)}) and I∘succ := (I(1),…,I(m)) : {0,…,m−1} → [P]. Claim: Σ_{I strictly increasing} ((α∧γ)(u_I))² ≤ c²·Σ_{J : {0,…,m−1}→[P] strictly increasing} γ(u_J)². In the statement each sum runs over all maps, with summand 0 for maps that are not strictly increasing.

1. (Wedge formula.) By ContinuousAlternatingMap.alternatizeUncurryFin_apply and (α.smulRight γ)(x) = α(x)·γ (ContinuousLinearMap.smulRight_apply), for w = (w_0,…,w_m):
 (α∧γ)(w) = Σ_{i=0}^{m} (−1)^i α(w_i)·γ(w_0,…,ŵ_i,…,w_m), where ŵ_i is omitted.

2. (Values on strictly increasing tuples.) Let I be strictly increasing and w := u_I. For 1 ≤ i ≤ m, I(i) > I(0) ≥ 0, so I(i) ≠ 0 and α(u_{I(i)}) = 0 by (H); the i-th term vanishes. Removing the 0-th entry of u_I leaves u_{I∘succ}, so the i = 0 term is (−1)^0·α(u_{I(0)})·γ(u_{I∘succ}). By (H), α(u_{I(0)}) = c if I(0) = 0 and 0 otherwise. Hence
 (α∧γ)(u_I) = c·γ(u_{I∘succ}) if I(0) = 0, and (α∧γ)(u_I) = 0 if I(0) ≠ 0.

3. (The left side.) Let A := {I : {0,…,m} → [P] : I strictly increasing and I(0) = 0}. By step 2, the left side equals Σ_{I∈A} c²·γ(u_{I∘succ})².

4. (Injection into increasing m-tuples.) For I ∈ A, I∘succ is strictly increasing, since it composes I with the strictly increasing map succ : j ↦ j+1. The map Φ : I ↦ I∘succ is injective on A. If I, I' ∈ A and I∘succ = I'∘succ, then I(0) = 0 = I'(0) and I(j+1) = I'(j+1) for all j < m, so I = I'.

5. (Estimate.) Let B := {J : {0,…,m−1} → [P] : J strictly increasing}. By step 4, Σ_{I∈A} γ(u_{I∘succ})² = Σ_{J∈Φ(A)} γ(u_J)². This is ≤ Σ_{J∈B} γ(u_J)², because Φ(A) ⊆ B and every summand is ≥ 0. Multiply by c² ≥ 0 and use step 3: the left side is ≤ c²·Σ_{J∈B} γ(u_J)², which is the right side of the claim.

6. (Degenerate cases.) If P = 0 there is no map {0,…,m} → [P], so the left side is 0, which is ≤ the nonnegative right side. If m+1 > P then A = ∅ and the left side is 0. The case m = 0 is included; then I∘succ is the empty map and γ is a 0-covector. ∎

Formalization pointers:
- Fin.sum_univ_succ isolates i = 0, and Fin.removeNth_zero gives removeNth 0 w = Fin.tail w.
- Strict monotonicity gives (I 0 : ℕ) < (I i.succ : ℕ) via Fin.succ_pos.
- Rewrite the left side as a sum over Finset.univ.filter (StrictMono I ∧ (I 0 : ℕ) = 0) using Finset.sum_filter.
- Then use Finset.sum_image with the injectivity of I ↦ (fun j ↦ I j.succ) (proved with Fin.cases), Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset_of_nonneg, and Fin.strictMono_succ.
proof_key_steps: (α∧γ)(w) = Σ_i (−1)^i α(w_i) γ(w with w_i removed), by alternatizeUncurryFin_apply and smulRight_apply.
For strictly increasing I, every term with i ≥ 1 vanishes (I(i) ≠ 0), so (α∧γ)(u_I) = c·γ(u_{I∘succ}) if I(0) = 0, and 0 otherwise.
The left side equals Σ_{I strictly increasing, I(0)=0} c²·γ(u_{I∘succ})².
I ↦ I∘succ is injective on {I(0) = 0} and lands in the strictly increasing m-tuples; nonnegativity gives ≤ c²·Σ_{J strictly increasing} γ(u_J)².

audit.reason: The one-line type matches the stated hypothesis and estimate for arbitrary u and real c. The verified wedge formula leaves only the initial-index-zero contribution. Deleting that index is injective on the restricted tuples, and nonnegative square sums give the inequality. No orthonormality or sign condition on c is needed; the degenerate cases are covered.

subproblem.title: Counting identity: Σ_{all I} φ(u_I)² = k!·Σ_{I strictly increasing} φ(u_I)² (parent Step 1)
subproblem.statement: For all P, k ∈ ℕ, every family u = (u_0,…,u_{P−1}) of vectors of ℝ^P (u : Fin P → Eucl P, arbitrary, not necessarily orthonormal) and every k-covector φ on ℝ^P (φ : Covector (Eucl P) k, a continuous alternating k-linear map (ℝ^P)^k → ℝ): Σ_{I : {0,…,k−1} → [P]} φ(u_{I(0)},…,u_{I(k−1)})² = k!·Σ_{I strictly increasing} φ(u_{I(0)},…,u_{I(k−1)})². Here [P] = {0,…,P−1}. In Lean the right-hand sum runs over all I : Fin k → Fin P, with summand 0 when I is not strictly increasing.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P k : ℕ) (u : Fin P → Eucl P) (φ : Covector (Eucl P) k), ∑ I : Fin k → Fin P, (φ (fun i => u (I i))) ^ 2 = (k.factorial : ℝ) * ∑ I : Fin k → Fin P, if StrictMono I then (φ (fun i => u (I i))) ^ 2 else 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, Step 1 (counting lemma), with the bijection and the sign computation written out.

Notation. [P] := {0,…,P−1}. u = (u_0,…,u_{P−1}) is an arbitrary family of vectors of ℝ^P; no orthonormality is used. φ is a k-covector, i.e. a continuous alternating k-linear map (ℝ^P)^k → ℝ. For I : {0,…,k−1} → [P] write u_I := (u_{I(0)},…,u_{I(k−1)}) and g(I) := φ(u_I)². Let Inc be the set of strictly increasing I and Inj the set of injective I. Let S_k be the group of permutations of {0,…,k−1}, so |S_k| = k!. The right-hand sum of the statement equals Σ_{β∈Inc} g(β), because its summand is g(I) for strictly increasing I and 0 otherwise. So the claim is Σ_{all I} g(I) = k!·Σ_{β∈Inc} g(β).

1. (Non-injective maps contribute 0.) Let I ∉ Inj and choose a ≠ b with I(a) = I(b). The tuple u_I then has the same vector in positions a and b, so j ↦ u_{I(j)} is not injective. Because φ is alternating, φ(u_I) = 0, so g(I) = 0. Hence Σ_{all I} g(I) = Σ_{I∈Inj} g(I).

2. (Permutation invariance.) For every I and σ ∈ S_k, u_{I∘σ} = u_I∘σ, the tuple u_I with its entries permuted by σ. Because φ is alternating, φ(u_I∘σ) = sign(σ)·φ(u_I) with sign(σ) ∈ {1, −1}. Therefore g(I∘σ) = sign(σ)²·φ(u_I)² = g(I).

3. (Parametrization of injective maps.) Define Φ : S_k × Inc → Inj by Φ(σ, β) := β∘σ.
 (a) Φ is well defined: β is strictly increasing, hence injective, and σ is bijective, so β∘σ is injective.
 (b) Φ is injective. Suppose β∘σ = β'∘σ'. Since σ and σ' are surjective, β and β' both have the image of β∘σ = β'∘σ' as their image. Two strictly increasing maps β, β' : {0,…,k−1} → [P] with the same image are equal. Indeed, if β ≠ β', let t be the least index with β(t) ≠ β'(t), say β(t) < β'(t). Then β(t) = β'(s) for some s. If s < t, then β'(s) = β(s) < β(t). If s ≥ t, then β'(s) ≥ β'(t) > β(t). Both are contradictions. So β = β'. Then β∘σ = β∘σ' and injectivity of β give σ = σ'.
 (c) Φ is surjective. Let I ∈ Inj. Its image s := I({0,…,k−1}) has exactly k elements. Let β be the increasing enumeration of s; it is a strictly increasing map {0,…,k−1} → [P] with image s, so β ∈ Inc. For each a, β(a) ∈ s, so β(a) = I(b) for a unique b =: τ(a). The map τ : {0,…,k−1} → {0,…,k−1} is injective because β is, so τ ∈ S_k, and I∘τ = β. Hence I = β∘τ⁻¹ = Φ(τ⁻¹, β).
 So Φ is a bijection.

4. (Summation.) Reindex along the bijection Φ (step 3), then use g(β∘σ) = g(β) (step 2):
 Σ_{I∈Inj} g(I) = Σ_{(σ,β)∈S_k×Inc} g(β∘σ) = Σ_{σ∈S_k} Σ_{β∈Inc} g(β) = k!·Σ_{β∈Inc} g(β).

5. (Conclusion.) Steps 1 and 4 give Σ_{all I} φ(u_I)² = k!·Σ_{β∈Inc} φ(u_β)² = k!·Σ_I (φ(u_I)² if I is strictly increasing, else 0). This is the claim. Degenerate cases are included. For k = 0, the only map is the empty map, which lies in both Inc and Inj, and |S_0| = 1 = 0!. For k > P, Inj = Inc = ∅ and both sides are 0. ∎

Formalization pointers (all present at the pinned Mathlib): ContinuousAlternatingMap.map_eq_zero_of_not_injective; AlternatingMap.map_perm applied to φ.toAlternatingMap; Tuple.sort, Tuple.monotone_sort, Monotone.strictMono_of_injective, Tuple.comp_perm_comp_sort_eq_comp_sort, Tuple.sort_eq_refl_iff_monotone (τ in step 3(c) can be taken as Tuple.sort I); Finset.sum_nbij' for the reindexing; Fintype.card_perm and Fintype.card_fin for |S_k| = k!.
proof_key_steps: Non-injective I give a tuple u_I with a repeated vector, so φ(u_I) = 0 because φ is alternating; the full sum reduces to injective I.
For a permutation σ, φ(u_{I∘σ}) = sign(σ)·φ(u_I), hence φ(u_{I∘σ})² = φ(u_I)².
(σ, β) ↦ β∘σ is a bijection from S_k × {strictly increasing β} onto the injective maps: equal images force β = β', and the increasing enumeration of the image gives surjectivity.
Σ_{I injective} φ(u_I)² = Σ_σ Σ_β φ(u_β)² = k!·Σ_{β strictly increasing} φ(u_β)².

subproblem.title: Slotwise Parseval: Σ_{all I} φ(u_I)² is the same for every orthonormal basis u (parent Step 2)
subproblem.statement: For all P, k ∈ ℕ, any two orthonormal bases u = (u_0,…,u_{P−1}) and v = (v_0,…,v_{P−1}) of ℝ^P (OrthonormalBasis (Fin P) ℝ (Eucl P)) and every k-covector φ on ℝ^P (Covector (Eucl P) k): Σ_{I : {0,…,k−1} → [P]} φ(u_{I(0)},…,u_{I(k−1)})² = Σ_{I : {0,…,k−1} → [P]} φ(v_{I(0)},…,v_{I(k−1)})². Both sums run over all index maps I : Fin k → Fin P.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P k : ℕ) (u v : OrthonormalBasis (Fin P) ℝ (Eucl P)) (φ : Covector (Eucl P) k), ∑ I : Fin k → Fin P, (φ (fun i => u (I i))) ^ 2 = ∑ I : Fin k → Fin P, (φ (fun i => v (I i))) ^ 2
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, Step 2 (basis independence of N). It is stated here for two arbitrary orthonormal bases u and v. The parent uses v = e, the standard basis; the argument is the same.

Notation. [P] := {0,…,P−1}; ⟨·,·⟩ and |·| are the Euclidean inner product and norm of ℝ^P. u = (u_0,…,u_{P−1}) and v = (v_0,…,v_{P−1}) are orthonormal bases of ℝ^P. φ is a k-covector, a continuous alternating k-linear map (ℝ^P)^k → ℝ; only multilinearity is used. For a family w and I : {0,…,k−1} → [P] put φ(w_I) := φ(w_{I(0)},…,w_{I(k−1)}) and N_w(φ) := Σ_{all I} φ(w_I)². Claim: N_u(φ) = N_v(φ).

1. (Parseval in one slot.) For every linear functional ℓ : ℝ^P → ℝ, Σ_{i∈[P]} ℓ(u_i)² = Σ_{i∈[P]} ℓ(v_i)². Proof: by the Riesz representation on ℝ^P, ℓ = ⟨a, ·⟩ for some a ∈ ℝ^P. For any orthonormal basis w of ℝ^P, a = Σ_i ⟨a, w_i⟩ w_i, so |a|² = Σ_i ⟨a, w_i⟩² (Parseval). Hence Σ_i ℓ(u_i)² = Σ_i ⟨a, u_i⟩² = |a|² = Σ_i ⟨a, v_i⟩² = Σ_i ℓ(v_i)². Both sums equal the squared operator norm ‖ℓ‖² = |a|²; every linear functional on ℝ^P is continuous.

2. (Hybrid sums.) For r = 0, 1, …, k and I : {0,…,k−1} → [P], let w^{r,I} be the k-tuple with entries w^{r,I}_j := v_{I(j)} for j < r and w^{r,I}_j := u_{I(j)} for j ≥ r. Put M_r := Σ_{all I} φ(w^{r,I})². Since w^{0,I} = u_I and w^{k,I} = v_I, M_0 = N_u(φ) and M_k = N_v(φ).

3. (One slot at a time: M_r = M_{r+1} for r < k.) Fix r < k. The maps I : {0,…,k−1} → [P] correspond bijectively to pairs (i, I'), where i := I(r) ∈ [P] and I' is the restriction of I to {0,…,k−1}∖{r}. For fixed I', set x_j := v_{I'(j)} for j < r and x_j := u_{I'(j)} for j > r. Define ℓ_{I'}(z) := φ(x_0,…,x_{r−1}, z, x_{r+1},…,x_{k−1}); this is a linear functional on ℝ^P because φ is linear in its r-th argument. If I corresponds to (i, I'), then w^{r,I} and w^{r+1,I} both have entry x_j in every position j ≠ r: for j < r both use v_{I(j)}, and for j > r both use u_{I(j)}. Their r-th entries are u_i and v_i respectively. Hence φ(w^{r,I}) = ℓ_{I'}(u_i) and φ(w^{r+1,I}) = ℓ_{I'}(v_i). Summing first over i ∈ [P] and then over I', and applying step 1 to each ℓ_{I'}:
 M_r = Σ_{I'} Σ_{i∈[P]} ℓ_{I'}(u_i)² = Σ_{I'} Σ_{i∈[P]} ℓ_{I'}(v_i)² = M_{r+1}.

4. (Conclusion.) By step 3, N_u(φ) = M_0 = M_1 = ⋯ = M_k = N_v(φ). For k = 0 the chain is trivial: both sides equal φ()², the value on the empty tuple. For P = 0 and k ≥ 1 both sums are empty. ∎

Remark (the same slot-by-slot replacement, organized for Lean). Run it as an induction on k, for all k-covectors at once. In degree k+1, write φ(z_0, z_1,…,z_k) = ψ_{z_0}(z_1,…,z_k), where ψ_z := φ(z, ·,…,·) is a k-covector (ContinuousAlternatingMap.curryLeft, curryLeft_apply_apply). Split I into (I(0), J) with J := (I(1),…,I(k)) (Fin.consEquiv, Fintype.sum_prod_type). Replace u by v in the last k slots by applying the induction hypothesis to each ψ_{u_i}. Exchange the two sums (Finset.sum_comm). Finally, replace u_i by v_i in slot 0 by step 1 applied to ℓ_J(z) := ψ_z(v_J), the continuous linear functional (ContinuousAlternatingMap.apply ℝ ℝ^P ℝ v_J) ∘ curryLeft φ. Step 1 is Mathlib's OrthonormalBasis.norm_dual: ‖ℓ‖² = Σ_i ℓ(w_i)² for every orthonormal basis w.
proof_key_steps: One-slot Parseval: for every linear functional ℓ = ⟨a,·⟩, Σ_i ℓ(u_i)² = |a|² = Σ_i ℓ(v_i)² (OrthonormalBasis.norm_dual).
Hybrid sums M_r use v in slots j < r and u in slots j ≥ r, so M_0 = N_u(φ) and M_k = N_v(φ).
M_r = M_{r+1}: fixing every index except I(r) makes slot r a linear functional ℓ_{I'}, and Σ_i ℓ_{I'}(u_i)² = Σ_i ℓ_{I'}(v_i)².
The chain M_0 = ⋯ = M_k gives N_u(φ) = N_v(φ).

subproblem.title: The Euclidean coefficient norm can be computed in any orthonormal basis (parent Step 3)
subproblem.statement: For all P, k ∈ ℕ, every orthonormal basis u = (u_0,…,u_{P−1}) of ℝ^P (OrthonormalBasis (Fin P) ℝ (Eucl P)) and every k-covector φ on ℝ^P (Covector (Eucl P) k): covectorEuclideanNorm(φ)² = Σ_{I : {0,…,k−1} → [P] strictly increasing} φ(u_{I(0)},…,u_{I(k−1)})². In Lean the sum runs over all I : Fin k → Fin P, with summand 0 for I that are not strictly increasing. So SimonGMT's coefficient norm, defined with the standard basis, takes the same value in every orthonormal basis.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P k : ℕ) (u : OrthonormalBasis (Fin P) ℝ (Eucl P)) (φ : Covector (Eucl P) k), covectorEuclideanNorm φ ^ 2 = ∑ I : Fin k → Fin P, if StrictMono I then (φ (fun i => u (I i))) ^ 2 else 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, Step 3. It uses the sibling results count_sq_sum (parent Step 1, Lean slicing_mb_wn_sq_sum_eq_factorial_mul) and parseval_sq_sum (parent Step 2, Lean slicing_mb_wn_sq_sum_onb_invariant).

Notation. e = (e_0,…,e_{P−1}) is the standard basis of ℝ^P (e_i = EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin P) ℝ i); it is an orthonormal basis. For a family w = (w_0,…,w_{P−1}) and a k-covector φ, put φ(w_I) := φ(w_{I(0)},…,w_{I(k−1)}), N_w(φ) := Σ_{all I : {0,…,k−1}→[P]} φ(w_I)² and Σ^<_w(φ) := Σ_I (φ(w_I)² if I is strictly increasing, else 0). Let u be an orthonormal basis of ℝ^P. Claim: covectorEuclideanNorm(φ)² = Σ^<_u(φ).

1. By definition, covectorEuclideanNorm(φ) = √(Σ^<_e(φ)). Every summand of Σ^<_e(φ) is a square or 0, so Σ^<_e(φ) ≥ 0. Therefore covectorEuclideanNorm(φ)² = Σ^<_e(φ).

2. Apply count_sq_sum to the family u (the basis vectors u_0,…,u_{P−1}) and to the family e: N_u(φ) = k!·Σ^<_u(φ) and N_e(φ) = k!·Σ^<_e(φ).

3. Apply parseval_sq_sum to the orthonormal bases u and e: N_u(φ) = N_e(φ).

4. Steps 2 and 3 give k!·Σ^<_u(φ) = k!·Σ^<_e(φ). Since k! ≥ 1, k! ≠ 0 and it cancels: Σ^<_u(φ) = Σ^<_e(φ). By step 1 this equals covectorEuclideanNorm(φ)². ∎

Formalization pointers: unfold covectorEuclideanNorm and use Real.sq_sqrt with Finset.sum_nonneg. The definition's summand is literally (φ (fun i ↦ EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin P) ℝ (I i))) ^ 2 under the same StrictMono decidability instance. So the sibling statements instantiated with the family ⇑(EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin P) ℝ), and with v := EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin P) ℝ, match it syntactically. Cancel with Nat.factorial_ne_zero and mul_left_cancel₀.
proof_key_steps: covectorEuclideanNorm(φ)² = Σ^<_e(φ), because the radicand is a sum of nonnegative terms.
count_sq_sum: N_u(φ) = k!·Σ^<_u(φ) and N_e(φ) = k!·Σ^<_e(φ).
parseval_sq_sum: N_u(φ) = N_e(φ).
Cancel k! ≠ 0: Σ^<_u(φ) = Σ^<_e(φ) = covectorEuclideanNorm(φ)².

audit.reason: The exact type matches the coefficient-norm identity. Nonnegativity justifies squaring the defining square root. The two declared dependencies identify the factorial-weighted sums, and the nonzero real cast of k! permits cancellation. No additional dependency or circular basis-invariance assumption is used.
